What Can Latent World Models Know?
Physical Parameter Identifiability
in Multimodal Predictive Representations

Kaizhen Tan Affiliation: New York University, New York, NY, USA Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, USA    Xin Xu Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, USA    Siru Tao Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, USA    Hanzhe Hong Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, USA    Yang Feng Affiliation: Columbia University, New York, NY, USA    Heqing Du Affiliation: Columbia University, New York, NY, USA
Abstract

A central premise of latent world models is that predicting the future forces a representation to internalize the physics of its environment. Which physical quantities does a trained latent actually contain, and what decides this? We answer with controlled interventions in PokeWorld, an interactive environment whose visually identical objects hide mass, drag, and contact stiffness. A certificate-gated protocol first certifies each parameter as recoverable from raw observations, then measures whether it enters the latent, so a null result can be attributed to the objective rather than to the environment. The resulting identifiability map has two organizing mechanisms and one frontier. Inputs limit what can be known, while prediction targets decide what is retained. Stiffness enters the latent only when touch is forecast (R2 0.500.50, against −0.02-0.02 when the same signal is merely fused into the input), and under single-step prediction a vision-only latent discards even perfectly visible object state. Drag marks the frontier. It carries a recoverability certificate of 0.890.89 yet plateaus near 0.130.13 under every deterministic prediction objective we test, while a supervised head on the same trunk reaches 0.450.45. Parameters whose readout is slow and ratio-type under the sensed coordinates fall outside what these objectives acquire. On RH20T, an input×\timestarget factorial over scaling curves reproduces both mechanisms across two robots and 4,2584{,}258 episodes. Every arm missing information or prediction pressure stays flat over a 5×5\times data range, and only the full multimodal objective forecasts force beyond a persistence baseline, with held-out gains that grow with scale. Objective structure determines which physical parameters a latent acquires, and additional data improves only the parameters it already acquires.

1 Introduction

A central promise of world models is that predicting the future forces a representation to internalize the physics of the environment (LeCun, 2022; Hafner et al., 2023; Assran et al., 2025). Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) make this promise concrete: an encoder maps observations to a latent state, a predictor rolls that state forward under actions, and both are trained by predicting future embeddings rather than pixels (Assran et al., 2023; Balestriero & LeCun, 2025; Maes et al., 2026). Such models now support visual understanding, prediction, and planning at scale (Assran et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024).

Yet the field cannot currently answer a basic scientific question: which physical quantities does the latent state of such a model contain, and what determines whether a given quantity is acquired? The answer matters practically—a manipulation policy that cannot estimate contact stiffness will fail exactly where contact-rich robotics is hardest—and theoretically, because prediction objectives acquire only what their targets require of them (Cui et al., 2026). Existing evaluations probe trained models post hoc (Garrido et al., 2025; Motamed et al., 2025) or establish that touch carries otherwise-missing evidence (Ye et al., 2026; Singh et al., 2026), but no prior work connects sensor streams, objective structure, and data distribution to the identifiability of individual physical parameters under controlled interventions.

This paper charts that map. We build PokeWorld, a minimal interactive environment in which a force-controlled agent pokes objects whose hidden parameters—mass mm, drag γ\gamma, contact stiffness kk—are resampled every episode and rendered identically: nothing about appearance reveals them. The three parameters deliberately span an observability spectrum (γ\gamma chiefly visual, mm cross-modal, kk almost purely tactile), so which representation acquires which parameter is diagnostic of the learning dynamics. Every claim passes the certificate gate: a recurrent probe on raw observations must certify a parameter as recoverable before any statement about a model is made. The gate separates environment defects from representation defects—and instrument defects from both—licensing the causal language used throughout.

On this substrate we train X-JEPA, a family of action-conditioned latent world models built on the heuristic-free LeJEPA/LeWM recipe (Balestriero & LeCun, 2025; Maes et al., 2026), factorially varying which modalities enter the input, which are prediction targets, and the horizon spectrum of prediction heads. Linear probes on the frozen predictor state, read against the recoverability certificates, measure what was learned. Four findings define the map, answering in turn what is recoverable, what the objective retains, and what stays systematically absent:

1. Target pressure is causal and modality-specific (§4.1). Contact stiffness enters the latent only when touch is a prediction target (R2 0.400.40–0.570.57 across seeds, regularization strengths, two architectures, and probe families)—not when touch is merely fused into the input (−0.02-0.02), nor when an equally sized proprioception target substitutes for it (−0.01-0.01). Mass rises monotonically with cross-modal pressure, and targets compose for object localization (0.580.58 vs. 0.170.17/0.090.09 alone).

2. Vision-only latent world models sit in a lazy equilibrium (§4.2). With single-step prediction they discard even directly visible, perfectly predictable object state (position R2 0.040.04)—visible, predictable, ignorable. Two independent mechanisms break the degeneracy—cross-modal targets (→0.58\rightarrow 0.58) and multi-horizon action-conditioned heads (→0.89\rightarrow 0.89)—and they compose (0.980.98); direct long-horizon heads also outpredict autoregressive composition at matched horizons (0.100.10 vs. 0.190.19 arena units; static 0.210.21).

3. The anti-collapse regularizer sets metric precision (§4.3). Sweeping the weight of SIGReg (the recipe’s sliced isotropic-Gaussian anti-collapse regularizer) over 60×60\times traces a monotone dose–response on every physical readout (stiffness 0.12→0.570.12\rightarrow 0.57; prediction error halves): distributional regularity trades against the latent’s metric precision, and low-intrinsic-dimension data wants an order-of-magnitude lighter regularization than image-scale defaults.

4. The map has a frontier (§4.5). Drag γ\gamma carries a recoverability certificate of R2 0.890.89 yet resists every prediction-side mechanism we deploy—across linear probes, nonlinear probes, and a functional test of the model’s own glide predictions—plateauing near 0.130.13. A supervised head on the same trunk reaches 0.450.45 with prediction quality unchanged, and a pixel-reconstruction variant is at least as blind: the failure sits with the deterministic prediction objectives we test, not with the environment or the probes. An attribute matrix with dose–response interventions then yields a two-regime picture: fast parameters are acquired through whatever computation their readout requires; slow parameters only up to their linear observational trace (a bias family swept over three signal levels tracks its linear certificate while its recurrent certificate stays near 0.950.95); and slow, ratio-type parameters, having no linear trace, are blind—immune even to a 30×30\times loss reweighting. Real-world parameters with this signature—viscosity, friction—are what contact-rich robotics needs; the frontier is a concrete target for the next generation of objectives.

Real-robot validation at scale (§5). On RH20T (Fang et al., 2023) across two embodiments (896896 and 4,2584{,}258 episodes), the map’s mechanisms transfer, evaluated on observables with held-out tasks throughout: the lazy equilibrium replicates verbatim; cross-modal targets improve dynamics prediction (−29%-29\% rollout error) and contact anticipation (AUC 0.70→0.800.70\rightarrow 0.80); force is retained, and forecast beyond a persistence baseline, only when touch is both fused and forecast. Camera viewpoint acts as an observable selector, a two-view model taking the union. Most consequentially, a four-arm factorial (inputs ×\times targets) run across within-embodiment scaling (800800–4,2584{,}258 episodes, fixed compute, +50%+50\%-compute control) separates sensor observability, input fusion, and prediction pressure: every arm missing a factor is flat in scale—the camera-only arms never gain force information no view carries, and the fused-input arm without cross-modal targets discards the force it is given—while the full objective is near-ceiling from 800800 episodes and converts additional scale into held-out-task gains. Scale cannot substitute for objective structure: multi-sensory pressure decides what can be learned, and only then does data decide how well.

Contributions. (1) PokeWorld and the certificate-gated identifiability protocol: a reusable methodology turning “what did the model learn?” into a controlled measurement. (2) The four-factor identifiability map—target causality, the lazy equilibrium and its escapes, the λ\lambda dose–response. (3) The frontier: a certificate-gated attribute-matrix characterization of what these objectives do not acquire, with objective-attribution controls. (4) Real-robot validation across two embodiments, culminating in a four-arm factorial over scaling curves showing that objective structure—not data volume—decides what is learned, with distilled design rules.

2 Related Work

Latent world models and JEPAs. Predicting future latent embeddings rather than observations underlies I-JEPA and V-JEPA (Assran et al., 2023; Assran et al., 2025), with action-conditioned variants supporting zero-shot planning (Assran et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024). LeJEPA replaces the stability heuristics of this line (EMA teachers, stop-gradients) with a single principled regularizer, SIGReg (Balestriero & LeCun, 2025), which LeWorldModel instantiates as a stable end-to-end pixel world model (Maes et al., 2026). We adopt this recipe as our substrate and contribute a systematic account of what its representations acquire—including a dose–response analysis that turns LeWM’s observation that SIGReg can struggle on low-complexity environments into an actionable tuning rule. Generative world models (Hafner et al., 2023) optimize reconstruction; we study the latent-predictive family and include a reconstruction-objective control on the same trunk (§4.5), which reproduces the blind region.

Touch and multimodal representation. Touch supplies physical evidence vision lacks: Sparsh learns self-supervised tactile representations (Higuera et al., 2024), TacGen shows contact-dependent properties become decodable only with a tactile channel (Ye et al., 2026), TouchWorld builds a generative visuo-tactile policy stack (Zhou et al., 2026), Kepler-Encoder fuses vision, proprioception, and force into a static multimodal embedding (Singh et al., 2026), and HPT scales proprioceptive–visual pretraining across embodiments (Wang et al., 2024). We study action-conditioned dynamics models and dissect the causal roles of inputs versus prediction targets—a distinction invisible to static-encoder studies, and one that reshapes how multimodal world models should be trained. Auxiliary prediction objectives shaping representations have RL antecedents (Jaderberg et al., 2017; Gelada et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2020); our contribution is the input-versus-target dissection under recoverability certificates, not target-driven content per se. Estimating physical parameters from video and interaction is likewise established (Wu et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2019): that line supplies the recoverability side, where we measure what prediction-trained latents acquire relative to it.

Physical understanding, probing, and identifiability. Benchmarks probe pretrained video models for intuitive physics (Garrido et al., 2025) and physical principles (Motamed et al., 2025); we complement post-hoc evaluation with a controlled methodology whose roots are classical: parameter identifiability and the role of input excitation are foundational in system identification (Ljung, 1999), and our certificates and behavior-policy design transpose them to learned latents. From the probing literature we import its central caution—probe results reflect probe capacity as much as representation content (Hewitt & Liang, 2019; Belinkov, 2022)—which is why every claim here is triangulated across linear probes, nonlinear probes, recoverability certificates, and functional prediction tests. The lazy equilibrium is a world-model instance of shortcut learning (Geirhos et al., 2020): the objective is satisfiable while ignoring task-relevant structure. On the theory side, JEPA objectives have been characterized as low-rank factorization of action-conditioned co-occurrences (Cui et al., 2026), SIGReg as an active-inference free energy (Arnez & Gomez-Villa, 2026), and data-averaged prediction error as insufficient to bound planner suboptimality (You et al., 2026); the lazy equilibrium, the blind region, and the scale-flat degeneracy supply concrete phenomena for such theories to explain.

3 PokeWorld and the Certificate-Gated Protocol

Environment. PokeWorld (Fig. 2) is a 2D arena in which a force-controlled circular finger interacts with an object under semi-implicit Euler dynamics with Hertzian-style penalty contacts (underdamped, ζ=0.25\zeta{=}0.25, so that impact transients survive). Each episode resamples hidden parameters—mass m∈[0.5,3.0]m\in[0.5,3.0], drag γ∈[0.5,4.0]\gamma\in[0.5,4.0] (velocity decay rate, mass-independent by construction), contact stiffness k∈[500,6000]k\in[500,6000]—while rendering is identical across episodes: nothing visual reveals any parameter (Fig. 7). Observations comprise vision, proprioception, and 7-d touch with sub-step statistics (mean, peak, and end-of-step force; contact duration): quasi-static push force is kk-independent, so stiffness lives only in impact transients—the band kHz force–torque sensors occupy and frame-averaging destroys. Behavior policies mix pursuit, strike–retreat, and free launches so contacts, impacts, and glides all occur. Which representation acquires which parameter therefore reads out the learning dynamics, not the environment (Fig. 2, middle).

Recoverability certificates. Before any model is evaluated, each parameter must be certified recoverable from raw observations (the full protocol is diagrammed in Fig. 6, appendix). A certificate is a lower bound: the best R2 achieved by any estimator we construct on raw observation windows—a supervised recurrent probe for all parameters (0.860.86 for log⁡m\log m, 0.870.87 for log⁡k\log k on contact windows) and, for drag, a physics-informed estimator reaching 0.890.89 where the recurrent probe reaches 0.700.70. Certificates let a null model result be attributed to the objective rather than the environment or the instrument; the estimator hierarchy is itself informative (linear probes cannot express the ratio m=F/am=F/a; windowed MLPs cannot express temporally gated programs; the recurrent probe expresses both, App. A). On the model side we report linear (ridge) and nonlinear (early-stopped MLP) probes on the frozen predictor state, plus functional tests of the model’s own predictions (§4.5). Throughout, we separate recoverable from observations (certificates), decodable from the latent (probes), and functionally used by predictions (glide tests)—never classical structural identifiability (Ljung, 1999): every statement is operational, under the tested models, coordinates, horizons, and objectives.

X-JEPA family. All models share the stable LeJEPA/LeWM substrate: per-frame encoders, a causal transformer predictor conditioned on actions, prediction heads at horizons Δ∈{1,4,16}\Delta\in\{1,4,16\}, and the SIGReg anti-collapse objective (weight λ\lambda; architecture in App. B). Variants factorially vary inputs (vision-only vs. all modalities) and targets (latent embeddings only; adding touch and/or proprioception forecasting), as tabulated in Fig. 2 (right). Models are ∼5{\sim}5M parameters and train in under an hour on a single laptop GPU—the entire study, including all real-robot experiments, was conducted on one RTX 4060.

Measurement. We probe the frozen predictor state with ridge regression for hidden parameters (on contact windows, where the certificates are established), object position and velocity, open-loop rollout and direct-Δ\Delta prediction against a static baseline, and, on real data, force readout, contact-onset anticipation (AUC), and held-out-task splits. All probe evaluations are episode-split: probe-fit and probe-test windows come from disjoint episode sets, and hidden parameters are resampled per episode.

4 The Identifiability Map

4.1 Targets, not inputs, decide content

Figure 3 shows the central factorial at λ=0.02\lambda{=}0.02 (two seeds; full table in Table 2, appendix). Three comparisons carry the causal weight:

(i) Touch as input does nothing for stiffness; touch as target does everything. VF fuses the full tactile stream into the encoder yet leaves kk at chance; VXt sees no touch at input yet reaches 0.400.40–0.430.43 by being asked to forecast touch: forecasting contact force under known actions requires the latent to carry stiffness—so it does.

(ii) The effect is modality-specific, not generic auxiliary pressure. VXp adds an equally sized proprioception-forecasting target and moves kk not at all (−0.01-0.01): what matters is not extra work, but that the extra work’s answer depends on the parameter. Early-stopped MLP probes reproduce every cell (0.40/0.44/0.510.40/0.44/0.51 for VXt/VX/VFX vs. ≤0.00\leq 0.00 for V/VXp; App. C): the ordering is invariant to probe capacity.

(iii) Targets compose. Neither single target localizes the object (position 0.170.17 and 0.090.09), but together they reach 0.580.58: the proprioception target pins the finger, the touch target pins the object relative to the finger, and the composition pins the object. Adding fusion (VFX) completes the picture (0.980.98 position, best mm, kk). The ordering reappears on real data (§5) and under a token-based encoder (dense aligned prediction lifts stiffness to 0.620.62): a property of the objective, not of one architecture. In precise form: inputs bound what can be known; prediction targets decide what is retained—for hidden parameters, fusion without forecasting contributes nothing.

4.2 The lazy equilibrium and its two escapes

Under single-step prediction, the vision-only latent barely contains the object: position R2 0.040.04, despite the object being large, visible, and trivially predictable. The equilibrium is self-consistent (a static object contributes almost no prediction loss, so the encoder drops it, so the jointly learned targets never demand it), and the anti-collapse regularizer cannot prevent it: it constrains the distribution of embeddings, not their content. Two independent interventions break it: cross-modal targets restore position to 0.580.58 (Table 2); multi-horizon action-conditioned heads (Δ∈{1,4,16}\Delta\in\{1,4,16\}) restore it to 0.890.89 with no additional modality—over 16 steps the object’s future position is a large, action-dependent effect the objective can no longer ignore—and the two compose to 0.980.98. The heads bring a second benefit: at matched horizon, the direct Δ=16\Delta{=}16 head decodes to 0.100.10 arena-unit error where autoregressive composition reaches 0.190.19 (static 0.210.21)—long-horizon prediction is best asked for directly, not assembled from rolled short steps. The equilibrium is a property of the tested class—single-step global-embedding prediction with jointly learned targets: dense token prediction restores position by construction (our token variant: 0.980.98), and masked architectures with frozen targets report positional competence (Garrido et al., 2025)—the degeneracy names the failure mode those designs avoid.

4.3 The regularizer sets metric precision

Figure 8 (appendix) sweeps λ\lambda over 60×60\times (full table in App. C). All probes trace the same monotone curve: the isotropic-Gaussian pressure that guarantees non-collapse also spreads a low-dimensional physical manifold across the full latent, and the spreading acts as metric noise on fine-grained readouts. Training remains stable across the entire range—the practical failure mode on low-intrinsic-dimension data is over-regularization, not collapse, and the fix is a one-knob adjustment. This turns a known qualitative concern (Maes et al., 2026) into a quantitative tuning rule, and doubles open-loop prediction quality for free.

4.4 Information, computation, and data coverage

Information bandwidth is set at the sensor: with frame-averaged touch, stiffness is unrecoverable even from raw observations—averaging destroys the impact transients—while sub-step tactile statistics restore the certificate to 0.870.87. Computation converts derivatives into measurements: a frozen self-supervised flow estimator as an input channel raises velocity readout from 0.790.79 to 0.880.88 on the same data and objective. Data coverage allocates the gradient mass acquisition runs on: the identical VFX objective trained on contact-poor data collapses stiffness from 0.500.50 to 0.050.05 and mass to 0.110.11—the objective can only identify parameters in regimes the data visits. With target pressure (§4.1), these complete the map’s four levers, each isolated by its own intervention.

4.5 The frontier: a certificate-gated blind region

Drag γ\gamma is where the map ends—and the certificate makes the ending informative: a physics-informed estimator certifies γ\gamma recoverable at 0.890.89 from state trajectories (0.430.43 from pixel-derived observables, App. C), a self-supervised flow sensor certifies the derivative information reaches the input, and multi-horizon heads certify long-horizon pressure. Yet across six families of prediction-side mechanisms (App. C), γ\gamma plateaus near 0.130.13 under both probe families, and a functional test shows the model’s own glide predictions are beaten by an estimator that simply assumes the population-median γ\gamma.

The failure is the objective’s—and not one objective’s. A supervised system-identification head (same trunk, data, optimizer) lifts γ\gamma from 0.120.12 to 0.450.45 (mass and stiffness likewise, Table 1) with 16-step prediction unchanged: the substrate carries the parameter the moment the objective asks. And swapping latent targets for pixel-reconstruction targets (a deconv decoder on the same trunk—the core signal of generative world models) leaves γ\gamma at least as blind (0.030.03–0.080.08 under both probe families) while replicating the touch-target mechanism (stiffness 0.610.61): blind region and target causality are shared by both deterministic point-prediction families we test, latent-target and pixel-target alike. The gap that remains between supervision (0.450.45) and certificate (0.890.89) marks what the current trunk and history length leave unrecovered even when the objective asks.

Where exactly does acquisition stop? Four candidate attributes distinguish γ\gamma from the learned parameters: slow (the parameter’s per-step effect on predicted observations lies below the per-channel noise floor—here, sub-pixel displacement and velocity increments below the readout residual; a fast parameter exceeds it within single events), ratio-type (its readout from the model’s observation coordinates requires divisions rather than linear functionals—an attribute of the parameter–sensor pair, not of the parameter alone), temporally gated (informative only on glide segments), and low variance-share. An attribute matrix plus two dose–response interventions separates all four. Each cell carries two certificates where they differ—a linear probe on raw windows (the parameter’s linearly-accumulable trace) and a recurrent probe (its full window-recoverable content); both are empirical lower bounds, so every ratio compares the model to the best estimator we constructed (quoted fractions are therefore upper bounds on the truly acquired share). Table 1 carries the result. Stiffness, the fast parameter, is acquired at 0.60.6–0.70.7 of its certificate although no linear functional reads it: when the parameter is fast, the objective installs whatever computation its readout needs. The additive bias family, swept over three signal levels at fixed structure, decides what slowness does: its recurrent certificate stays near 0.950.95 at every level, yet the model tracks the linear certificate instead—a slow parameter is acquired only through its linear trace. The two slow×\timesratio parameters, which have no linear trace, are not acquired at all. And variance-share is a throttle, not a key:

a 30×30\times reallocation toward glide raises γ\gamma’s decodability only 0.08→0.270.08\rightarrow 0.27 while its functional test worsens, and starving the contact-frame touch loss drives stiffness to zero, parameter-specifically, with data and certificates unchanged (App. C). This is the blind-region hypothesis, an empirical hypothesis about deterministic prediction objectives under these observation coordinates: fast parameters are acquired as needed; slow parameters only through their linear trace; slow, ratio-type parameters not at all. (The certificate gate polices the matrix itself—it rejected three entangled constructions and forced the two-certificate protocol, App. C.)

The hypothesis makes a falsifiable coordinate-level prediction: attributes belong to the parameter–sensor pair, so a coordinate in which drag’s trace becomes linear should unblind it. A log-speed input channel does exactly that (Δ​log⁡|v|=−γ​Δ​t\Delta\log|v|=-\gamma\,\Delta t on glide): γ\gamma’s linear certificate rises from ≈0{\approx}0 to 0.520.52 and the readout follows to 0.330.33—0.640.64 of it, the fraction at which every linearly-traced parameter is acquired (App. C). Functional use in position forecasts, which still requires exponentiating the trace, does not follow. Mass calibrates a fifth lever, target precision: nominally fast×\timesratio, it reads at 0.430.43 of its pixel certificate where stiffness reads at 0.640.64–0.790.79—its trace routes through the SIGReg-regularized latent target (the λ\lambda dose–response, §4.3, is its throttle), stiffness’s through raw-valued touch heads.

A mechanism consistent with every cell is conditional-mean collapse: under squared-error point prediction, whatever a short history does not pin down is optimally answered by predicting under the population mean of the parameter, so nothing pressures an episode-specific belief. The matrix reads naturally in these terms. Fast parameters sharpen the within-window posterior enough that the optimal prediction needs them. Additive parameters leak a linear trace into short-horizon states, and the model carries exactly that trace—it tracks its linear certificate across the bias sweep, never its recurrent one. Slow×\timesratio parameters, whose effect on the loss within any prediction horizon stays below the noise floor, are answered by the prior mean—which also explains why a 30×30\times loss reweighting raises decodability without creating functional use. A heteroscedastic Gaussian-NLL variant, which reweights gradients but leaves the mean-optimum unchanged, moves nothing (γ\gamma 0.100.10 vs. 0.120.12)—as the mechanism requires; objectives whose optimum is not a conditional mean (episode-level latent variables, belief states) remain the discriminating test.

Beyond the frontier, the same lens applies to viscosity, damping, and friction—with the caveat the definition already carries: the attributes belong to the parameter–sensor pair. Whether friction is fast or slow depends on the sensing (stick–slip transients are fast; smooth sliding is not), and charting exactly that is what the map and its certificates are for.

4.6 Control utility tracks state content

The map’s content transfers to closed-loop control, and control decomposes along the map’s rows: model-predictive control on the frozen latents (same planner, budget, and environment for every representation; planner and episode in App. C.4, Fig. 10) reaches the goal region in 20%20\% of episodes for the object-blind vision-only latent, 3838–44%44\% when either target composition restores object state (VXt/VXp), and 𝟓𝟕%\mathbf{57\%} for the full model (random: 1%1\%; distance metric in App. C.4). Matched state content yields matched control whether or not the latent carries stiffness: the position-goal task discriminates state acquisition only, and force-limited manipulation is the natural next benchmark.

5 Real-Robot Data: the Mechanisms Transfer

Real scenes carry no ground-truth mass or stiffness, so this section tests whether the map’s mechanisms—lazy equilibrium, target pressure, fusion, and their scaling behavior—govern real multimodal streams. We port the recipe unchanged to RH20T (Fang et al., 2023): a KUKA and a Flexiv arm (896896 and 4,2584{,}258 episodes; corpus details App. C.5), 1010 Hz, single 96×9696{\times}96 camera unless stated; episode-level splits, every headline metric also reported on entirely held-out tasks. Metrics are observation-space: force and end-effector position readout from the latent, open-loop and direct 16-step prediction vs. a static baseline, and contact-onset anticipation (AUC; definition in App. C.5). By the map’s own bandwidth lever, 1010 Hz force sampling removes stiffness-type transients: the contact-parameter frontier is out of reach on this corpus by construction, and what transfers is the mechanism set.

The lazy equilibrium replicates; targets improve dynamics. Vision-only V loses end-effector state (position 0.760.76 IID, 0.480.48 OOD) and predicts worse than static (8.28.2 vs. 3.83.8 cm). Cross-modal targets (VX, VXt) cut rollout error up to 29%29\% and lift anticipation AUC 0.70→0.800.70\rightarrow 0.80—the toy’s target-pressure mechanism on real streams.

Fusion under target pressure delivers force; viewpoint selects observables. With force–torque fused and forecast as a target, VFX retains force (0.870.87; OOD 0.560.56), predicts 16 steps at 1.51.5 cm (2.5×2.5\times better than static), and anticipates contact at AUC 0.860.86. For camera-only latents the camera decides what can be known: a far view carries pose but not contact, a close-up the reverse, and a two-view model takes the union (per-viewpoint numbers in App. C.5). Viewpoint is an observable selector, multi-view its union operator.

The factorial at scale: scale cannot buy back what the objective refuses. Readout metrics on fused-input models can be input-driven, so we bound the trivial component first: an untrained copy of the fused architecture, probed identically, already reads force at 0.940.94 and position at 0.970.97—random projections pass inputs through. Read against this bound, the 2×22{\times}2 factorial (inputs ×\times targets), run across within-embodiment scaling (800800–4,2584{,}258 episodes at fixed compute, with a +50%+50\%-compute control), assigns every metric its cause (Fig. 5; App. C). Position readout is passthrough: the fused arms sit at the bound at every scale, and the vision-only model sits at its own random-feature bound across the whole range—more compute does not change this. Force is where the factorial bites, and forecasting is its honest metric: current-force readout is passthrough-bounded, so the center panel asks the passthrough-immune question instead—predict force 0.40.4 s ahead. VFX beats the persistence baseline at every scale and its forecast improves with data (0.39→0.510.39\rightarrow 0.51 held-out)—the one metric where scale clearly pays (episode-bootstrap CIs, App. C); VX stays below persistence at every scale, because no amount of data supplies information the camera does not carry. The retention view (Fig. 11, appendix) confirms the factorial: VF, which receives force as an input, lands far below the untrained bound (0.150.15 vs. 0.910.91)—training compresses away a sensed modality nothing pressures it to keep. The same signature runs through every learning metric: direct 16-step error improves monotonically as factors add (12.0→2.312.0\rightarrow 2.3 cm; static 3.33.3), and camera-only anticipation is learned (AUC 0.62→0.770.62\rightarrow 0.77) while fused-model anticipation sits at its random-feature bound. Cross-robot differences that look like scale effects are the viewpoint lever again (App. C.5). Objective structure decides what can be learned; data decides only how well.

One model, two robots. A single configuration-blind VFX trained jointly on both corpora (no robot identifier) matches both specialists on position and anticipation and lifts the data-poor KUKA side’s force retention from 0.560.56 to 0.89\mathbf{0.89} on held-out tasks: pooled cross-embodiment experience supplies the task coverage that stabilizes retention. Another robot’s experience is not interference but coverage.

6 Design Rules

The map compresses into rules, each backed by a controlled comparison:

  1. 1.

    Every modality a prediction target—un-forecast fusion is discarded; forecast touch to know stiffness.

  2. 2.

    Sense at the physics’ bandwidth—sub-step tactile statistics, motion channels, derivative estimators.

  3. 3.

    Ask for the future at multiple horizons, directly—breaks the lazy equilibrium; beats autoregressive composition.

  4. 4.

    Tune anti-collapse to the data’s intrinsic dimension—an order of magnitude lighter on physical data.

  5. 5.

    Structure first, scale second—arms missing information or pressure stay flat across a 5×5\times range.

7 Limitations

Both tested objectives are deterministic point predictions on one trunk. Objectives whose optimum is not a conditional mean, such as episode-level latent variables or belief states, are the discriminating test for the mechanism we propose, and they lie outside the family this study scopes; our Gaussian-NLL control is the closest variant we run, and it moves γ\gamma not at all. Blind-region statements are scoped accordingly. Second, the real-robot sections validate the map’s mechanisms on observables rather than parameter identifiability itself, since RH20T has no ground-truth object parameters; the direct test is a corpus of objects with known, varied physical parameters. Third, models are ∼5{\sim}5M parameters on one GPU: what transfers is the protocol, not the ceiling.

8 Conclusion

We asked which physical quantities a prediction-trained latent contains. Certificates separate what the environment affords from what the objective acquires, and under that separation the answer is narrower than the premise we started from. A latent carries the parameters its prediction targets require of it, while a modality that is fused but never forecast contributes nothing. Additional data changes this in no arm that lacks either the information or the prediction pressure. One class of certified-recoverable parameters is acquired by none of the objectives we test, and naming that class precisely is what the environment and its certificates are for.

Reproducibility statement

The environment, protocol, and all evaluation code run on one consumer GPU; exact configurations are in the appendix, and code will be released.

Appendix A Environment and Protocol Details

Dynamics. Bodies follow semi-implicit Euler integration at d​t=0.05\mathrm{d}t{=}0.05 with 20 substeps. The finger (mass 11, radius 0.060.06) is driven by a commanded force Fmax​atF_{\max}a_{t}, at∈[−1,1]2a_{t}\in[-1,1]^{2}; the object (radius 0.090.09) experiences drag force −γ​m​v-\gamma mv (so the velocity decay rate γ\gamma is mass-independent by construction), and finger–object contact follows a Hertzian penalty law Fc=k​d3/2F_{c}=k\,d^{3/2} with normal damping at ζ=0.25\zeta{=}0.25 of critical, where dd is the overlap. Underdamping matters: near-critical damping makes impact peaks damping-dominated and suppresses the stiffness signature that the tactile channel must carry. Parameters are sampled log-uniformly (m∈[0.5,3]m\in[0.5,3], k∈[500,6000]k\in[500,6000]) or uniformly (γ∈[0.5,4]\gamma\in[0.5,4]) per episode.

Sensors. Vision renders anti-aliased 64×6464{\times}64 grayscale; the model input adds a temporal-difference channel. Proprioception is finger position and velocity (4-d). Touch reports per-control-step sub-step statistics of the reaction force on the finger: mean force (2-d), peak magnitude, end-of-step force (2-d), contact duration fraction, and a contact flag (7-d total). Sensor noise σ=0.02\sigma{=}0.02 is added to force channels.

Behavior policy. Episodes (64 steps) mix three modes with random switching—pursuit (sustained pushes), strike–retreat cycles (clean impacts followed by free glides), and Ornstein–Uhlenbeck drift—plus a fraction of episodes in which the object is launched with random velocity, so that contacts, impacts, and glides all appear in the marginal data distribution.

The oracle estimator. The oracle is a 2-layer GRU (width 96) over 16-step windows of raw observations, trained directly on the parameter labels. Gates require contact-window R2 of at least 0.4/0.4/0.250.4/0.4/0.25 for m/γ/km/\gamma/k before any model result is interpreted.

Instrument hierarchy. Instrument choice is itself part of the protocol. A linear probe on raw windows cannot express the ratio m=F/am=F/a and scores near zero on all three parameters. A windowed MLP recovers mass (0.450.45) but scores 0.00.0 on drag, even though a hand-written estimator (the median log velocity-ratio over glide frames) reaches 0.890.89: drag is a temporally gated program that flat architectures do not express. The recurrent oracle expresses both program classes and sets the certificates used throughout (0.86/0.70/0.870.86/0.70/0.87). Certificate estimators read trajectories of finger state (proprioception), touch, actions, and object state; object state is privileged relative to the pixel channel, and pixel-derived counterparts are reported in App. C. The same discipline applies on the model side: reported probes are ridge regressions, so every claimed acquisition is linearly available in the latent, and the functional glide test (App. C) separately checks whether the model’s own predictions use a parameter.

Appendix B Training Details

Architecture. All models share per-frame encoders—a 4-stage CNN (channels 32/64/128/25632/64/128/256, stride 2) over the frame and temporal-difference channels, with small MLPs for proprioception and touch—fused and projected through a linear layer with BatchNorm. There is deliberately no trailing LayerNorm: a final LayerNorm constrains embeddings to a shell and blocks the isotropic-Gaussian target of SIGReg, reproducing the observation of Maes et al. (2026). The predictor is a 4-layer causal transformer (width 192, 8 heads, dropout 0.1) with zero-initialized AdaLN action conditioning. Prediction heads at Δ∈{1,4,16}\Delta\in\{1,4,16\} condition on the flattened intervening action window, and cross-modal forecasting heads (touch, proprioception) sit on the trunk where the variant specifies. The latent dimension is 128.

Optimization. AdamW at learning rate 3×10−43{\times}10^{-4} with cosine decay and 500-step warmup, weight decay 0.050.05, batches of 96–128 windows of 24 frames, 20k steps, bf16 autocast. SIGReg uses 1024 random directions with 17 integration knots, resampled every step.

Token-level SIGReg. For token-based variants, SIGReg is evaluated on 4096 subsampled token rows with 256 directions per step. Per-step resampling preserves coverage while cutting the regularizer’s activation memory by two orders of magnitude—the change that makes token-level SIGReg practical at all.

Control variants. The reconstruction control replaces the latent targets with a shared deconvolutional decoder (four stride-2 upconvolutions from a 4×44{\times}4 map, channels 256/128/64/32256/128/64/32) fed by per-horizon adapters (action-conditioned for Δ>1\Delta>1), decoding 8 uniformly subsampled positions per window and horizon; the touch and proprioception forecasting heads remain active, so only the visual latent target changes. SIGReg is omitted there, since pixel targets anchor the latent. The system-identification control adds a 2-layer head from the trunk to whitened (log⁡m,γ,log⁡k)(\log m,\gamma,\log k) at loss weight 0.50.5.

Runtime. Toy models train in 30–45 minutes and real-data models in about 45 minutes on one RTX 4060 laptop GPU.

Appendix C Full Results

This appendix expands every number cited in the main text into full tables, organized so that each subsection reads stand-alone: §C.1 covers the PokeWorld factorial, both probe families, and the regularizer sweep; §C.2 the attribute matrix, its constructions, and the two loss-share dose–responses; §C.3 the objective-attribution controls; §C.4 closed-loop planning; and §C.5 the complete real-robot results, including the untrained-encoder bounds.

C.1 PokeWorld: the factorial, both probe families, and the regularizer

Table 2 is the central input×\timestarget factorial at the λ=0.02\lambda{=}0.02 operating point, two seeds per variant, with the recoverability certificates in the last row.

The ordering is robust in three directions. It is unchanged at λ=0.1\lambda{=}0.1 and under a token-based encoder, where dense spatially aligned Δ=1\Delta{=}1 prediction lifts stiffness further, to 0.620.62. Position probes for all multi-horizon variants lie in 0.950.95–0.980.98, and open-loop 8-step decoded error spans 0.0620.062–0.0820.082 arena units against a static baseline of 0.1090.109. And the same ordering holds under nonlinear probes: early-stopped MLP readouts reproduce every cell, with γ\gamma at chance under both probe families.

A note on the position column of Table 2: it reports the single-horizon operating point, where the lazy equilibrium is visible (§4.2); VF’s position under fused inputs is passthrough-dominated, so its informative version appears in the real-data factorial (§C.5).

Finally, the data-coverage intervention of §4.4: the identical VFX objective trained on 95%-glide data and evaluated on the standard probe distribution falls to log⁡k\log k 0.050.05, log⁡m\log m 0.110.11, position 0.870.87, velocity 0.580.58, against 0.50/0.29/0.98/0.790.50/0.29/0.98/0.79 with standard coverage—acquisition runs on the gradient mass the data supplies.

C.2 The attribute matrix and its dose–responses

The matrix asks which attributes of a physical parameter decide whether a prediction-trained latent acquires it. Each cell pairs a parameter with its recoverability certificate (the appropriate instrument per cell: GRU sequence probes for ratio-type parameters, linear and GRU probes for the linear cells, the physics-informed estimator for drag) and scores acquisition as model readout over certificate—a comparison to the best simple estimator, since certificates are lower bounds.

Down the bias family the model tracks its linear certificate and never its recurrent one, which stays near 0.950.95 at every signal level; the fast parameter alone is acquired beyond its linear trace. The two dose–responses below rule out variance-share as the missing explanation.

The coordinate test. Supplying a log-speed input channel (computed from the frozen flow sensor) linearizes glide decay. The linear γ\gamma certificate under this coordinate—ridge regression on log-speed sequences over glide windows (696/351696/351 fit/test)—is 0.520.52, and the trained model’s glide-window readout rises from 0.080.08 to 0.330.33 (ridge; the MLP probe is unstable on this small subset), with stiffness, mass, and velocity unchanged. The functional glide test does not improve (0.1140.114 against a median-γ\gamma reference of 0.0540.054): the linear trace is acquired; its exponentiation into position forecasts is not.

Pixel-derived certificates. Replacing simulator object state with pixel-centroid estimates (finger disk masked using proprioception, 3-frame smoothing): the recurrent certificate reads m/γ/k=0.72/0.43/0.78m/\gamma/k=0.72/0.43/0.78 (state-based 0.86/0.70/0.870.86/0.70/0.87), and a centroid-based analytic γ\gamma estimator degrades to 0.050.05—sub-pixel velocity precision is the binding constraint. Model readouts against pixel certificates: stiffness 0.640.64–0.790.79, mass 0.430.43, drag 0.300.30.

Constructing the cells. The slow×\timeslinear cell required four constructions; the certificate gate rejected the first three, each instructively: (i) a per-episode drift acceleration is unrecoverable from 16-step windows because it enters v˙=ad−γ​v\dot{v}=a_{d}-\gamma v jointly with per-episode drag (certificate 0.030.03); (ii) fixing γ\gamma still fails a linear certificate because the drift is readable only on contact-free frames—temporal gating again; (iii) a multiplicative actuation gain is inherently ratio-type (g=Δ​v/(F​a)g=\Delta v/(Fa); certificate −0.00-0.00). The accepted construction is an additive per-episode force bias on the agent: Δ​v=(F​a+b−c​v)​d​t\Delta v=(Fa+b-cv)\,\mathrm{d}t is linear in (a,v,b)(a,v,b), ungated, and sub-pixel per step. Its linear certificate is 0.130.13; the recurrent certificate (0.920.92) later exposed how loose that bound is, which is what motivated the two-certificate protocol and the three-level sweep in the table. The rejected actuation gain then serves as the slow×\timesratio×\timesungated cell in its own right: regenerated as a dedicated corpus (g∈[0.85,1.15]g\in[0.85,1.15] multiplying the commanded force), its linear certificate fails as designed (−0.013-0.013) while a GRU sequence certificate recovers it at 0.6890.689; the trained model’s trunk reads it at −0.011-0.011 (ridge) / −0.010-0.010 (MLP)—none of its recurrent certificate—in a run whose stiffness, mass, and position probes are at normal levels (0.340.34/0.200.20/0.960.96).

Dose–response 1: reweighting toward the blind parameter. Sampling zero-contact (glide) episodes at relative weights {1,4,16,64}\{1,4,16,64\} reallocates the expected loss mass of glide segments from 32%32\% to 97%97\%, with data, probe sets, and certificates unchanged. Linear decodability of γ\gamma creeps upward but never approaches its certificate (0.890.89); the functional glide test worsens; and the acquired parameters pay the price.

Dose–response 2: starving an acquired parameter. Scaling the contact-frame touch-loss weight down from its default drives stiffness to exactly zero, parameter-specifically—mass dips mildly and γ\gamma does not move—again with data and certificates unchanged.

Together: loss share is a continuous throttle on parameters the objective can acquire, and no amount of it unblinds the slow×\timesratio conjunction.

The γ\gamma intervention ledger (Fig. 9). For completeness, every prediction-side mechanism deployed against drag, with its outcome: multi-horizon heads (γ\gamma: 0.00→0.050.00\rightarrow 0.05), a motion input channel (→0.12\rightarrow 0.12 plateau), spatial tokens (no gain), magnitude-weighted motion-forecast targets (no gain), a frozen flow velocity sensor (velocity readout 0.79→0.880.79\rightarrow 0.88; the γ\gamma plateau unchanged), and glide-enriched data (no gain). The functional test evaluates the model’s own direct 16-step predictions on certified pure-glide windows against analytic references: an estimator that knows the true γ\gamma errs by 0.00020.0002, one that assumes the population-median γ\gamma by 0.0490.049, a static predictor by 0.1440.144; the model sits above the median-γ\gamma reference at every loss share (Dose–response 1). γ\gamma-specific information is absent functionally, not merely linearly.

C.3 Objective-attribution controls

Both controls keep the VFX trunk, data, probes, and optimizer, and change only the objective. The supervised system-identification head shows the substrate carries every parameter the moment the objective asks for it; the reconstruction objective shows the blind region is not specific to latent targets, while the touch-target mechanism transfers.

The reconstruction rows have no direct-16 entry because their latent prediction heads receive no gradient (App. B); the probes are the comparable quantity. The Gaussian-NLL row is the minimal belief-adjacent variant: heteroscedastic variance heads reweight gradients (velocity and position readouts improve) but leave the conditional-mean optimum—and the blind region—unchanged.

Composition probes. At the multi-horizon operating point, finger, object, and relative object–finger position probes saturate for every variant (0.960.96–1.001.00): the composition effect of §4.1 belongs to the single-horizon regime of Table 2, where multi-horizon pressure is absent and object position differentiates (0.09/0.17/0.580.09/0.17/0.58).

C.4 Closed-loop planning

Push-to-goal with the same planner, budget, and environment for every representation (§4.6): CEM over smooth two-knot action programs, scored by the direct Δ=4/16\Delta{=}4/16 heads, replanning every 4 steps; Fig. 10 contrasts two representations on one held-out episode. Deployment follows the map: smooth action candidates (forward heads respond faithfully where trained) and direct-Δ\Delta scoring, not composed rollouts (§4.2).

C.5 Real-robot results in full

Three protocol notes apply throughout. Sensor streams are per-column clipped to robust ranges (0.10.1–99.999.9 percentiles) before whitening. Contact-onset labels mark ‖F‖>10\|F\|>10 N within the next 4 steps; onset base rates differ across configurations (2.75%2.75\% on cfg7, 0.64%0.64\% on cfg1), so AUC values compare within, not across, configurations. Every IID/OOD pair is a probe-episode / held-out-task split.

The pilot configuration (KUKA, cfg7). Far camera; 896896 episodes, 5656 tasks, static baseline 3.83.8 cm.

Viewpoint study (cfg7). Rows report the camera-only quantities at each viewpoint: force from VX, position from the best camera-only variant at that viewpoint. VFX is stable across all three (0.980.98 position, 0.840.84–0.900.90 force).

Scaling within one embodiment (Flexiv, cfg1). The numbers behind Fig. 5; static baseline 3.33.3 cm. At full scale the +50%+50\%-compute control leaves V’s position at 0.160.16, and V’s open-loop 16-step rollout is 15.715.7 cm.

Cross-robot differences are a viewpoint effect. The apparent V degradation across robots is the viewpoint effect of Table 11, not a scale effect.

Untrained-encoder bounds. Random weights, identical probe protocol: frame-level readout of fused inputs is passthrough, and prediction is not. Figure 11 plots the four arms’ current-force readout against this bound—the retention view of the factorial whose learning view (forecasting) appears in Fig. 5.

Future-force forecasting. R2 of predicted force at t+Δt{+}\Delta (IID/OOD) against a persistence baseline that repeats the last observed force. Forecasting is the passthrough-immune force metric: VFX doubles the persistence baseline at 0.40.4 s while camera-only VX cannot match it.

Across the scaling arms, VFX’s held-out Δ=4\Delta{=}4 forecast rises 0.39→0.50→0.510.39\rightarrow 0.50\rightarrow 0.51 (800/2,000/4,258800/2{,}000/4{,}258 episodes) while VX sits at −0.05/−0.11/−0.05-0.05/-0.11/-0.05: the center panel of Fig. 5 in numbers. Paired episode-bootstrap 95%95\% CIs of the model−-persistence difference exclude zero at every scale for VFX ([+0.01,+0.17][+0.01,+0.17] at 800800; [+0.14,+0.28][+0.14,+0.28] at 4,2584{,}258) and are strictly negative for VX ([−0.55,−0.15][-0.55,-0.15]), so neither the advantage nor its growth with scale is a task-composition artifact.
